solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Drive OAP mad, taking home too much (8)

annotation.definitionNote: The answer is an adjective; the definition is a participle phrase describing the same state, as in 'the boss is overpaid / taking home too much'.

indicatorNotes.mad: going mad means losing order, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A pensioner being driven up the wall by someone who earns far too much.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Drive' looks like the verb of 'drive mad', but it is only letters. An OAP (old-age pensioner) is a British term for a retired person.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone overpaid takes home more pay than they deserve.

entries.clue: Watch old boy start to rally (7)

blocks.note: OB is the standard abbreviation for old boy, a former pupil
in tennis, the serve is what starts a rally

annotation.surface: A former pupil watching a tennis rally get under way.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Start to rally' reads like the first letter of 'rally', but it is a whole word: the serve is what begins each rally.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to watch something closely is to take note of it with the eyes.

entries.clue: Poet in loo briefly keeling over (5)

indicatorNotes.briefly: a brief word is cut short, so the last letter goes
indicatorNotes.keeling over: a boat keeling over turns upside down, so in a down clue the letters run backwards

blocks.note: loo = TOILET, cut short to TOILE
reversal indicator: the shortened loo is read upwards

annotation.surface: A poet collapsing in the lavatory.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like it puts something inside the loo, but it only joins the definition to the wordplay. T. S. Eliot wrote The Waste Land.
annotation.definitionFit: T. S. Eliot is one of the best-known poets of the twentieth century.

entries.clue: Unrealistic hope of something to eat on plane (3,2,3,3)

blocks.note: the idiom for a hope that will never come true
taken literally: a plane flies high above, so food served on board is up there too

annotation.surface: Wishing for a decent meal on an aeroplane.
annotation.walkthrough: The second half reads the idiom literally: a plane is in the sky, so a pie served on board is a pie in the sky. The joke is that airline food is itself an unrealistic hope.
annotation.definitionFit: Pie in the sky is a promise or hope that is very unlikely to be realised.

entries.clue: Small creature quietly escaping from vet (6)

indicatorNotes.escaping from: what escapes from a word leaves it, so P is removed

blocks.note: to vet something is to inspect it
p = piano, quietly in music; removed

annotation.surface: A small animal slipping silently out of the veterinary surgery.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Vet' pulls toward the animal doctor, which suits 'small creature', but here it is the verb meaning check.
annotation.definitionFit: Beetles, ants and flies are the small creatures this class of animal covers.

indicatorNotes.hiding in: the answer is hiding inside the next word

blocks.note: the four letters after 'cup' in the word

annotation.surface: A prickly character tucked away in a cupboard.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Customer' in the sense of an awkward type ('a tough customer') here means an animal; a wild boar has a bristly coat.
annotation.definitionFit: A boar is a hairy, bristle-coated pig, and 'customer' is slang for a character or creature.

entries.clue: Up before the judge, as footballer might be? (2,5)

blocks.note: being tried in court
a player being tried out by a club before signing is in this state

annotation.surface: A footballer in court, which happens often enough to be a newspaper staple.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the second sense as an example: a footballer on trial is being tried out, not tried for a crime.
annotation.definitionFit: A legal phrase for a defendant facing the court, and a sports phrase for a player being tried out by a club.

indicatorNotes.about: to go about something is to surround it

blocks.note: to rave is to rage
n = new; RAGE goes around it

annotation.surface: Someone raving about their new Aga cooker.
annotation.walkthrough: 'New Aga' suggests an anagram of AGA, but 'new' is just N. An Aga is a British brand of heavy cast-iron cooking range; the question mark flags it as an example.
annotation.definitionFit: An Aga is one make of range, a large kitchen stove.

indicatorNotes.The Speaker’s: what a speaker says is heard, not read, so the word is the sound

blocks.note: sweet = delightful; said aloud it matches a word for a set of rooms

annotation.surface: The rooms reserved for the Speaker of the House of Commons are lovely.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The Speaker' looks like the House of Commons official, which makes 'Speaker's accommodation' seem a single phrase; the Speaker only signals a sound-alike.
annotation.definitionFit: A suite is a set of rooms, as in a hotel.

entries.clue: Article on southern constituent, one from Greece (7)

indicatorNotes.on: in an across clue, one thing on another comes after it

blocks.note: s = southern
a constituent is a part of something
an is the indefinite article

annotation.surface: A news article about a voter in the south of the country.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Constituent' suggests a voter in a constituency, but here it means a component.
annotation.definitionFit: A Spartan comes from Sparta, a city of ancient Greece.

entries.clue: Having nothing to do, doctor eats a noodle (2,1,5,3)

indicatorNotes.doctor: to doctor something is to tamper with it, so the letters are altered

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 11 letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A bored doctor snacking on noodles to pass the time.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' reads as the person eating, but it is the verb that scrambles the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom for idleness, from a rope's end left loose with no task to secure.

indicatorNotes.losing head: the head of a word is its first letter, which goes

blocks.note: TROT is short for Trotskyist, a far-left socialist; its T is dropped

annotation.surface: A heckler dismissing a socialist's speech as rubbish, or wondering if he has lost his head.
annotation.walkthrough: TROT, short for Trotskyist, is a common crossword word for a left-winger.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for nonsense, as in 'talking rot'.

indicatorNotes.demolished: a demolished building is knocked apart, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Someone wolfing a whole tin of fruit.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Demolished' in the surface means eaten up, which is why it hides so well as the scrambling signal.
annotation.definitionFit: A nectarine is a smooth-skinned fruit like a peach.

indicatorNotes.close to: the close of a word is its end, so take its last letter

blocks.note: an earth is a fox's burrow
last letter of property

annotation.surface: A rough tunnel dug right up against someone's land.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Close to' reads as 'near', but it means the close, or end, of the next word. An earth is the name for a fox's den.
annotation.definitionFit: Humour that is down-to-earth and bawdy gets called this, a plain synonym of crude.

blocks.note: to rap is to rebuke or criticise
port is the left side of a ship

annotation.surface: Attacking the political left's grasp of an issue.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Left' reads as the political left, but it is the nautical side. The ’s stands for 'has', joining the wordplay to the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Rapport is a close, sympathetic understanding between people.

indicatorNotes.away from: what goes away from a word leaves it, so R is removed

blocks.note: the old word for a coal miner, from coal; its final R is what runs away
r = runs, from cricket scoring; removed

annotation.surface: A dog fleeing from a miner.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Runs away' reads as one phrase about the dog, but 'runs' is the letter R and 'away from' does the removing.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: a Scottish sheepdog breed, such as the Border breed.

blocks.note: ex = former, as in ex-wife
the press = journalists collectively

annotation.surface: Retired reporters travelling by rail.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like it places one piece inside another, but it only links the wordplay to the definition. 'Maybe' marks an express train as one kind of express.
annotation.definitionFit: An express is a fast train that makes few stops.

entries.clue: Provide evidence of watching Lord’s match? (6)

blocks.note: a spectator watching the game is at it
a Test is an international cricket match, and Lord's is the London cricket ground where many are played

annotation.surface: Asking for proof that someone really went to the cricket.
annotation.walkthrough: Lord's is a famous cricket ground in London; the question mark admits that 'watching' only loosely means 'at'.
annotation.definitionFit: A formal verb for testifying, as a witness does when signing a document.

entries.clue: They’re said to attract night and day, perhaps (9)

blocks.note: from the proverb about magnets and couples
night and day are an example: each is the reverse of the other

annotation.surface: Romance between two people as different as night and day.
annotation.walkthrough: The first half needs the proverb 'opposites attract'; 'perhaps' marks night and day as one example.
annotation.definitionFit: Night and day are opposites, and opposites are proverbially drawn together.

indicatorNotes.Some: only some of the next word is used

blocks.note: five letters after 'nymph' in the word

annotation.surface: Asking whether a certain man-mad woman comes from the Persian Gulf.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that Omani is only one nationality from the Gulf; Oman lies on the Arabian Peninsula.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone Omani comes from Oman, a Gulf state.

blocks.note: to outdo a story, as in 'to top that'
a peaked hat

annotation.surface: Donald Trump's baseball hat.
annotation.walkthrough: Trump looks like the president, whose red cap is famous, but it is the verb meaning outdo; the ’s stands for 'is'.
annotation.definitionFit: To cap something is to trump it; a cap is also a piece of headgear.

blocks.note: a car is a vehicle
scarper is British slang for run off, go

annotation.surface: A getaway: pack the car and run.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Load' reads as a verb in the surface, but it is the noun definition. Scarper is British slang for run away.
annotation.definitionFit: Cargo is a load of goods carried by a vehicle or ship.

indicatorNotes.surprisingly: letters arranged in a surprising way are rearranged

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Someone meant to stay impartial who gets unexpectedly cross.
annotation.walkthrough: The two ends contradict each other in the surface, a neutral party getting annoyed, which is the clue's small joke.
annotation.definitionFit: Anodyne means bland and inoffensive, unlikely to provoke either side.

entries.clue: Strange European found in Great Lake (5)

blocks.note: e = European
Lake Erie is one of the Great Lakes of North America

annotation.surface: A weird European turning up in one of the Great Lakes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Found in' looks like an instruction to put E inside ERIE, but E simply comes first; the phrase just joins definition to wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for weird or uncanny.

blocks.note: the ninth letter of the Greek alphabet, the equivalent of our I
a tiny amount, as in 'not one jot'

annotation.surface: A Greek speaker saying 'I bit'.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a person confessing to biting, but 'I' is the letter and 'bit' is a noun meaning a small amount.
annotation.definitionFit: Iota is the Greek letter I, and because it is the smallest letter it also means a tiny bit.

indicatorNotes.attending: to attend someone is to accompany them, so US goes next to STUDIO

blocks.note: an artist works in a studio
US = American

annotation.surface: A learned American visiting a painter's workshop.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Attending' reads as going to the premises, but it just places US alongside STUDIO.
annotation.definitionFit: A studious person is devoted to study, that is, scholarly.
